## A Democratic Paradox

. . .

{{< video images/undecided_voters.mp4 >}}

## A Democratic Paradox

. . .

Classic and early-modern philosophers looked down on what we would recognize as democracy as rule by some combination of:

::: incremental
-   the mob (risks demagogues)
-   the poor (risks wealth redistribution)
-   the incompetent (risks generally bad decisionmaking)
:::

. . .

The people cannot be trusted to govern themselves.

. . .

And yet, people tend to value democracy as a form of government and it's done pretty well over the last couple of centuries.

```{=html}
<!--
## A Democratic Paradox

Quick show of hands: can you name your member of Congress (wherever you'd vote)? 

. . . 

What about your state senator?

-->
```

## Why this matters

Why do proponents of democracy think it's better than the alternatives?

::: incremental
-   Fundamental right to self-determination
-   Aggregation of private interests promotes the public good
    -   Democracy solves information problems
-   Democratic citizenship is self-actualizing *for democratic citizens*
:::

## Why this matters

But this only works if citizens have sufficient information and capacity to:

::: incremental
-   Be aware of and understand relevant issues
-   Know what they (should) want
-   Reason together about what they should do
:::

## Why this matters

Mass ignorance leaves three options:

::: incremental
-   Reject democracy
-   Limit the scope of self-determination
-   Strengthen democratic citizenship
:::

## Expectations of Democratic Citizenship

Last week I said that democracy isn't either/or.

There are different types of democracy, and systems can be more or less democratic.

. . .

Democratic theories vary in how much they expect of democratic citizens.

Democratic citizens were expected to deliberate on public matters, serve in public offices, and hold administrative responsibilities...though citizenship was strictly limited.

## Escaping the State of Nature

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
The core problem is that humans begin in the state of nature

::: {.fragment fragment-index="2"}
-   "war of all against all"
-   life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short"
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index="2"}
![Hobbes's Leviathan](images/leviathan_frontispiece.jpeg){width="80%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Frontispiece for The Leviathan. The Leviathan is depicted as looming over the city, comprised of individual people, wearing a crown and wielding a sword (for civil authority) and crosier (for religious authority). Additional symbols of civil power are in panels on the lower left and additional symbols of religious power are in panels on the lower right."}
:::
::::
:::::::

## State of Nature as Prisoner's Dilemma {.smaller}

|               | P2 Cooperates | P2 Fights |
|:-------------:|:-------------:|:---------:|
| P1 Cooperates |      2,2      |    0,3    |
|   P1 Fights   |      3,0      |    1,1    |

. . .

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
P1's ranking:

-   P1 exploits P2
-   Peace (both cooperate)
-   War (both fight)
-   P2 exploits P1
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
P2's ranking:

-   P2 exploits P1
-   Peace (both cooperate)
-   War (both fight)
-   P1 exploits P2
:::
:::::

. . .

Peace is [Pareto optimal]{.yellow} (no alternative makes everyone better off)

War is [equilibrium]{.yellow} (no alternative is individually rational)

## Collective Action Problem (Preview) {.smaller}

The prisoner's dilemma is a type of [collective action problem]{.yellow}, or situation in which individually rational decisions produce socially sub-optimal outcomes

. . .

Collective action problems are fundamental to politics, particularly at scale

-   How to arrive at a collective decision
-   How to ensure that this decision will be carried out

. . .

Tend to emerge with respect to public/collective goods, such as peace/security[and clean air, academic peer review, group assignments, party planning...]{.fragment}

## The Social Contract {.smaller}

::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="50%"}
The social contract solves the previous prisoner's dilemma with an (implicit) agreement to trade some freedom for cooperation-enforcing institutions.

:::: {.fragment fragment-index="2"}
Those institutions:

::: incremental
-   preserve private rights (safety, e.g.)
-   derive their authority from the people
:::
::::
:::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/leviathan_frontispiece.jpeg){width="80%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Frontispiece for The Leviathan. The Leviathan is depicted as looming over the city, comprised of individual people, wearing a crown and wielding a sword (for civil authority) and crosier (for religious authority). Additional symbols of civil power are in panels on the lower left and additional symbols of religious power are in panels on the lower right."}
:::
:::::::

::::: columns

The goal of the social contract is to escape the state of nature -- much lower bar than the Greeks' pursuit of common good.

## The Social Contract and the Emergence of Liberal Democracy

This makes elections useful for two things:

. . .

-   Select high ability citizens as representatives
-   Check their power / throw them out if necessary

. . .

This offers a "thin" model of democratic citizenship. [All it asks is for occasional votes to protect one's private interest.]{.fragment}

. . .

But it is extended to more people who can limit government's excesses.

Scholars often call citizenship in the United States "thin"

. . .

Our institutions reflect the (small-l) liberal democratic social contract tradition

. . .

Emphases:

-   indirect input on decisions via voting
-   protection of private rights and liberties
-   few *responsibilities* oriented toward the public good

## Democratic Citizenship in the United States

Competing traditions in U.S. political culture:

::: incremental
-   Skepticism of mass politics
-   Expectation of civic virtue
-   Faith in the individual/private sphere
-   Protectionist belief in voting as a check on centralized power
-   Communitarian belief in participation as self-actualizing (virtuous cycle)
:::

## Democratic Citizenship in the United States

This suggests a patchwork conception of democratic citizenship

. . .

Values both public good and pursuit of private interest

. . .

Varying expectations regarding the civic knowledge, virtue, and participation

## Democratic Citizenship in the United States

We treat political knowledge and civic virtue as resources[...without cultivating and distributing them.]{.fragment}

. . .

Result: unequal distribution of information, knowledge, and opportunity for authentic self-rule.

## Civic Virtue as a Collective Action Problem {.smaller}

Civic virtue as a resource we collectively cultivate --\> information/participation becomes a matter of collective action

. . .

How so? [Think of some direct/immediate *individual* costs...]{.fragment}

::: incremental
-   Time to collect and process information
    -   Developing coherent belief system takes effort
    -   Evaluating candidates/issues takes effort
-   Time to discuss politics with peers
-   Time/resources to go vote
    -   or contact representative, attend public meeting, protest, etc.
:::

## Civic Virtue as a Collective Action Problem {.smaller}

The benefits of participation tend to be indirect/*collective*. [If you participate...]{.fragment}

::: incremental
-   Your candidate you like *might* win/the one you don't *might* lose
    -   You need a bunch of other people like you to show up too
        -   But the odds your vote is decisive are slim
    -   If your candidate wins, they *might* move policy in your direction
-   Your protest *might* advance its cause
    -   Odds are better if it's a big movement
        -   But the bigger it is, the less it hinges on you
-   Improved/shared understanding has limited direct *material* value
:::

## Civic Virtue as a Collective Action Problem

Result: inequalities in information/participation

"Rational ignorance" when marginal cost of acquiring information \> marginal benefit of using it

![](images/first_amendment_annenberg.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Chart of percentage of people who can name specific protections of the First Amendment. 74% correctly name freedom of speech, 39% freedom of religion, 29% freedom of the press, 27% right of assembly, and 11% right of petition. 22% incorrectly name right to bear arms (that's the Second Amendment)"}

## This is Fine (?)

Consider:

::: incremental
-   Trivia isn't politics
-   Elite representation
-   Parties reduce complexity
-   "Collective rationality"
-   "Low-information rationality"
-   Ignorance is bliss
-   Full information doesn't exist
:::

## Why This is Not Fine

These points will come back later in the semester. They're good points! But we shouldn't be satisfied with them.

. . .

Capacity for civic virtue -- i.e. how much we *can expect* from citizens -- is a resource that can be cultivated and distributed.

. . .

One implication: the "democratic paradox" isn't a paradox.[..the less capable citizens are, the]{.fragment}[less democratic]{.yellow} society is.

## Types of Collective Action Problems

We just explored a specific collective action problem. Some broader categories:

-   Free rider
-   Tragedy of the commons
-   Prisoner's dilemma
-   Principal-agent

## Excludability and Rivalry

Some flavor of collective action is involved when managing goods that are...

-   [non-excludable]{.yellow}: can't prevent others from consuming good once it exists
-   [non-rival]{.yellow}: my consumption doesn't limit your consumption

## Types of Goods

|   | Rival | Non-Rival |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Excludable** | Private goods (food, cars) | Club goods (HOAs, unions) |
| **Non-Excludable** | Common-pool goods (parks, roads) | Public goods (defense, air) |

## Free Rider Problem

. . .

Occurs when individual contribution seen as unnecessary for public good production.

-   rational ignorance
-   group projects
-   academic peer review

## Tragedy of the Commons

. . .

Occurs when cost to consume a common pool resource is absent/insufficient to moderate consumption.

-   deforestation
-   overfishing
-   air pollution

## Prisoner's Dilemma

|                    | P2 Stays Quiet |   P2 Confesses   |
|:------------------:|:--------------:|:----------------:|
| **P1 Stays Quiet** | 1 year, 1 year |  10 years, Free  |
|  **P1 Confesses**  | Free, 10 years | 5 years, 5 years |

. . .

Variations:

::: incremental
-   Repeated game
-   Losses or gains?
-   More than two players
-   Institutions (that make defection costly)
:::

## Student's Dilemma

![](images/116_ec.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Extra credit question from a previous final: 'Please write either two or five, indicating the number of extra credit points you would like to receive on this exam. If up to 1/4 of those who respond ask for five points, everyone will get the extra credit they ask for. If more than 1/4 of those who respond ask for five points, no one will get any extra credit. Writing down anything other than two or five will be considered abstention (i.e. you will not receive any extra credit and we will subtract you from the denominator when determining the 1/4 threshold for others). There are 32 students in this class. Assuming everyone writes down either two or five, this means that up to eight students can receive five points of extra credit, but if more than eight students ask for five points then no one gets any extra credit. If one student abstains, that threshold drops to seven."}

## Principal-Agent Problem

. . .

Occurs when player delegating action (principal) and player to whom action is delegated (agent) have differing goals/incentives

::: incremental
-   bureaucracy (executive --\> bureaucrats)
-   elections (voters --\> politicians)
-   political campaigns (candidate --\> consultants, volunteers)
:::

## Coordination

Before we talk about specific solutions...

If I asked you to meet another student on campus, but you didn't know who, where, or when to meet...where and when would you go?

. . .

Why would this work?

. . .

Focal points aid in coordination.

## Solutions to Collective Action Problems

When spontaneous coordination isn't possible (which is often), we use institutions!

::: incremental
-   Ability to monitor, reward, and sanction
-   Can vary in how formal they are
-   Benefit from repeated iterations
    -   Norms develop over time
    -   Actors develop reputations
:::

## Examples of Institutions?

::: incremental
-   Congress
-   political parties
-   Krzyzewskiville
:::

## Coercion {.smaller}

. . .

Institutions limit some behaviors (coercion) to enable others (cooperation)

. . .

Rewards

::: incremental
-   Incentivize good performance
    -   tax credits for *behavior*
-   Privatization (property rights backed by state)
:::

Sanction

::: incremental
-   Compel contribution
    -   taxes for *revenue*
-   Regulation
:::

## Path Dependence

. . .

Results of coordination can stick long after they become inefficient:

::: incremental
-   imperial measurement vs. metric system
-   UK + colonies driving on left (wrong) side of the road
-   QWERTY keyboard
    -   Why QWERTY?
:::

. . .

Reflects power dynamics present at time of coordination (QWERTY due to merger of five largest typewriter companies in 1893)

-   [Transaction costs]{.yellow}: costs associated with making a collective decision
-   [Conformity costs]{.yellow}: the extent to which collective decisions constrain participants

## Essay 3 Prompt: The Public{.smaller}

Early in the semester we discussed a collective action problem at the core of democracy: it is a system of government that relies on people using information to contribute to collective decisions, but for any given individual the costs of acquiring true, important, and useful information are typically not worth the benefits. This is often referred to as "rational ignorance."

Each week in this section of the course will cover a different element of "the public" -- individuals, political parties, political candidates, interest groups, and the media. [Your assignment is to explain how the public can (in theory) address rational ignorance from the perspective of/with an emphasis on *one* of these elements.]{.yellow}

Successful essays will engage with multiple weeks of material, as elements of the public necessarily interact, but in order to keep things manageable one element of the public should remain the primary focus.

## Big Picture{.smaller}

Four big ideas

::: {.incremental}

1. Public opinion is more than the sum of its parts
    i) Surveys are useful-but-incomplete proxies
    ii) Social science is hard
2. People contain multitudes
    i) Mass attitudes have signal and noise
3. Random sampling is beautiful
    i) And really hard to approximate
4. No such thing as a perfect question
    i) But some questions are better than others

:::

# Public opinion is more than the sum of its parts

## What is public opinion?{.smaller}

. . .

Not clear that there's a single right answer!

. . .

Key (1961): "...those opinions held by private persons which governments find it prudent to heed."

. . .

In the bigger picture...

::: {.incremental}

*   what does it mean to have an opinion?
    + general disposition? specific stance? articulated reason?
    + retrieved ("file-drawer") or constructed?
*   what does it mean for that opinion to be public?
    + tallied or publicly articulated/justified?
*   how hell-bent is the majority?

:::

## "Public" vs. "Mass" Opinion{.smaller}

Mass opinion: "the product of a purely formal [arithmetic operation]{.yellow} by which typically poorly informed, casually maintained, critically unexamined, and [privately held considerations]{.yellow} about politics are [aggregated]{.yellow} by the pollster into an [ersatz vox populi]{.yellow}." - Gregory Markus (1994)

## The opinion survey

Surveys are pretty weird when you think about them.

. . .

Sort of like a conversation, but typically...

::: {.incremental}

*   strictly limits vocabulary
*   standardizes meaning
*   flattens differences in certainty/intensity
*   aggregates to point estimates

:::

. . .

More useful for some questions than others.

<!--

## Key terms in mass opinion

::: {.incremental}

*   Attitude: [latent/general construct in long-term memory]{.fragment}
*   Preference: [specific opinion on policy issue/area]{.fragment}
*   Stance: [position for/against a specific proposal]{.fragment}
*   Consideration: [discrete piece of information]{.fragment}
    + Potential reason for/against something

:::

## Models of Answering Survey Questions{.smaller}

Not the same thing as models of public opinion!

::: {.incremental}

*   [R]{.yellow}eceive, [A]{.yellow}ccept, [S]{.yellow}ample
    + Considerations accepted/rejected based on predispositions
      - Some people have more/stronger predispositions than others
    + Response is weighted average of considerations at "top of the head"
    + Events/context influence which considerations are available
*   On-line processing
    + Information affects summary judgment but isn't stored
*   Heuristics
    + Shortcuts to navigate unfamiliar/complex issues
    + Efficient, but not always accurate
    
:::

-->

## Material Interest vs. Ideology

Individuals are often [cross-pressured]{.yellow}

![](images/marble_nall_housing.png){fig-alt="Paper title page. Title: Where Self-Interest Trumps Ideology: Liberal Homeowners and Local Opposition to Housing Development; Authors: William Marble (Stanford University) and Clayton Nall (University of California, Santa Barbara). Abstract: How much does self-interest drive Americans’ policy attitudes? Survey research typically finds that self-interest’s role is minimal. Such conclusions are typically reached by examining attitudes toward federal policies that present diffuse costs and low stakes. We consider a starker test case of self-interest: controversies surrounding development of dense and affordable housing in Americans’ communities. Liberal homeowners, especially, must cope with dissonance between their egalitarian ideology and a desire to protect their home values and quality of life. They often embrace liberal housing goals and redistributive housing policies but join conservatives in opposing dense housing in their own communities. Two survey experiments show that liberal homeowners are cross-pressured and barely more likely than conservative homeowners to support dense housing development. Messages appealing to homeowners’ self-interest reduce support further, while countervailing appeals about housing’s benefits to low- and middle-income families barely offset the negative effect. We discuss implications for the politics of equal opportunity at the state and local level."}

## Sorting: absence of cross-pressures

Partisan [sorting]{.yellow} when more identities/preferences/values point in same political direction

## People *Really* Contain Multitudes

![](images/ahler_2014_abstract.png){width=80% fig-align="center" fig-alt="Paper title page. Title: Self-Fulfilling Misperceptions of Public Polarization. Author: Douglas J. Ahler. Abstract: Mass media convey deep divisions among citizens despite scant evidence for such ideological polarization. Do ordinary citizens perceive themselves to be more extreme and divided than they actually are? If so, what are the ramifications of such misperception? A representative sample from California provides evidence that voters from both sides of the state’s political divide perceive both their liberal and conservative peers’ positions as more extreme than they actually are, implying inaccurate beliefs about polarization. A second study again demonstrates this finding with an online sample and presents evidence that misperception of mass-level extremity can affect individuals’ own policy opinions. Experimental participants randomly assigned to learn the actual average policy-related predispositions of liberal and conservative Americans later report opinions that are 8–13% more moderate, on average. Thus, citizens appear to consider peers’ positions within public debate when forming their own opinions and adopt slightly more extreme positions as a consequence."}

## Measuring Mass Opinion: Sampling

Central Limit Theorem: Regardless of how a population is distributed, the [means of repeated samples]{.yellow} from that population will [trend toward being normally distributed]{.yellow}.

. . .

We can use sampling to apply the properties of the normal distribution to other distributions that are not symmetric or continuous (like vote choice).

. . .

Hear me out.

## Measuring Mass Opinion: Sampling{.smaller}

The Central Limit Theorem helps us *quantify uncertainty*

::: {.incremental}

*   [p-value]{.yellow}: [given a "null" hypothesis (of, say, 0), how (im)probable would the value we observed be *under repeated sampling*]{.fragment}
*   [confidence interval]{.yellow}: [*under repeated sampling*, this interval around the estimate will contain the true population parameter x% of the time]{.fragment}
    + [margin of error]{.yellow}: convention for describing confidence interval (often 95%)

:::

## Measuring Mass Opinion: Sampling{.smaller}

Alternatives to simple random sampling:

::: {.incremental}

*   Stratified random sampling
    + divide population into subgroups, randomly sample within subgroup
*   Cluster sampling
    + randomly sample within specific sub-units
*   Quota sampling
    + sample within strata until reaching pre-set N
*   Oversampling
    + collect more units from specific strata of interest

:::

## Exit Quiz Answers

1. Briefly (one sentence) explain the concept of "latent opinion."

. . .

Public opinion that will exist in the future, conditional on actions taken now.

## Exit Quiz Answers

2. True or false: Feldman and Zaller argue that most people "innocent" of ideology, in that they do not understand or use ideological values to inform their beliefs.

. . .

False.

## Exit Quiz Answers

3. Matt Grossman summarizes Soroka and Wlezien's work by saying "It may not be the failures of democratic politics that produce an ungrateful, seemingly vindictive public, but actually its successes." What does he mean (again, briefly!)?

. . .

Policy tends to move farther than what the public as a whole wants, generating a reaction in the opposite direction.

"The public learns what policy makers are doing, but that means less people demanding more of that and more demanding less."

## Measuring Mass Opinion: Sampling{.smaller}

What can we do if we know the sample isn't random? [It depends on whether we know *how* it isn't random.]{.fragment}

. . .

[Non-response bias]{.yellow}: when the propensity to respond, conditional on contact, systematically differs across the population of interest

. . .

![](images/rcp_trump_biden.png){width=50% fig-align="center" fig-alt="Real Clear Politics 2020 presidential election polling average, showing a consistent Biden lead of 5-10 percentage points (peaking at 10.2 points on June 23, 2020). Biden won the popular vote by roughly four percentage points."}

## Measuring Mass Opinion: Weighting

In practice, sampling is never truly random.

. . .

If we can *observe* the ways it is non-random, we can adjust.

. . .

The task: render people in the sample [statistically exchangeable]{.yellow} with people outside of it.

## Measuring Mass Opinion: Weighting{.smaller}

Lots of different ways to do this. Some common ones:

::: {.incremental}

*   "Raking" to population benchmarks
    + Upweight underrepresented cases, downweight overrepresented cases
*   "Matching" to target sample
    + Pair target sample cases with most similar observed cases, discard remaining (unrepresentative) observations
*   Inverse-propensity scoring
    + Upweight cases less likely to respond, downweight cases more likely to respond

:::

. . .

*All* weighting methods assume you have [observed everything that rendered the sample non-random]{.yellow}. [No matter how fancy your method is, it won't work without good data.]{.fragment}

## When in Doubt, Take an Average{.smaller}

A single poll is just that:

*   One sample
*   One set of questions
*   One set of analysis decisions
    + Sampling frame
    + Likely voter screen
    + Weighting

Different, reasonable decisions at each step can lead to different conclusions

. . .

Important to triangulate across multiple surveys

Context matters. This is often framed as a bug, but it's really a *feature*.

## Question Wording

Question wording reflects *choices* about relevant information.

|-|--------|--|

Question wording reflects *choices* about relevant information.

| % Pro | Question | Pollster|
|-|--------|--|
| 57 | Do you favor or oppose a temporary ban on refugees from Syria, Iraq, Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, and Yemen until the federal government improves its ability to [screen out potential terrorists]{.yellow} from coming here? | Rasmussen|
| 55 | Do you approve or disapprove of [President Trump's]{.yellow} executive order prohibiting citizens from seven predominantly Muslim countries from [being able to enter the United States for 90 days]{.yellow} and [halting processing of refugees for 120 days]{.yellow}? | Politico|
| 46 | Do you support or oppose [suspending all travel]{.yellow} by [citizens]{.yellow} of Iraq, Syria, Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, and Yemen to the U.S. for 90 days? | Quinnipiac|
| 42 | [Thinking about some of the specific actions Donald Trump has taken since he has been in office]{.yellow}, would you say you approve or disapprove of ordering a temporary ban on entry into the U.S. for [most people]{.yellow} from seven [predominantly Muslim countries]{.yellow}? | Gallup|

## Question Wording

Keeping constant wording over time can be more informative than perfecting the wording each time

![](images/gallup_abortion_trend.png){fig-alt="Gallup trend line for the question: Do you think abortions should be legal under any circumstances, legal only under certain circumstances, or illegal in all circumstnaces? Trend line for % Legal under any circumstnaces, highlighted, was 21% in 1975 and is typically in the mid-20s, but jumped from 25% to 34% between 2019 and 2024."}

## Framing

Choice of how to present issue

::: {.incremental}

*   Equivalence framing (90% employment vs. 10% unemployment)
*   Emphasis framing (KKK rally as free speech or public safety issue)
    + "welfare" vs. "aid to poor", e.g.
    + *counter*frames may cancel each other out

:::

. . .

Experimenting with different frames in same survey can be more informative than single frame

Easier for a turn of phrase to change the "object of evaluation" than the "evaluation of the object"

## Framing

Experimenting with different frames in same survey can be more informative than single frame

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](images/nyt_buses_headline.png){fig-alt="New Yorkers Support Free Buses, but They Don't THink it should Happen. A polling experiment shows how a small change in wording can make a big difference."}

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

![](images/nyt_buses_exp.png){fig-alt="Bar chart showing that wording changes policy support in New York City. For most issues, like adding police or making buses free, more people 'support' a policy than say 'N.Y.C. should do this'"}

:::

::::

## Question Order

What you ask about first can affect what your respondents think about later

. . .

Classic example: should the [U.S./Soviet Union] allow journalists from the [Soviet Union/U.S.] to enter?

::: {.incremental}

*   U.S. --> Soviet Union first: freedom of the press
*   Soviet Union --> U.S. first: national security

:::

. . .

First question changes the implied meaning of the second.

## Social Desirability

Respondents may be reluctant to express views that violate social norms

::: {.incremental}

*   can ask about these views *in*directly
*   may be less of an issue in online samples (evaluate case-by-case)
*   sensitivity to social norms may be empirically interesting!

:::

## Example: Shy Trump Voters?

![](images/coppock_shy_trump_voters.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Journal article title page. Title: Did Shy Trump Supporters Bias the 2016 Polls? Evidence from a Nationally-representative List Experiment. Author: Alexander Coppock. Abstract: Explanations for the failure to predict Donald Trump's win in the 2016 Presidential election sometimes include the 'Shy Trump Supporter' hypothesis, according to which some Trump supporters succumb to social desirability bias and hide their vote preference from pollsters. I evaluate this hypothesis by comparing direct question and list experimental estimates of Trump support in a nationally representative survey of 5,290 American adults fielded from September 2 to September 13, 2016. Of these, 32.5% report supporting Trump’s candidacy. A list experiment conducted on the same respondents yields an estimate 29.6%, suggesting that Trump's poll numbers were not artificially deflated by social desirability bias as the list experiment estimate is actually lower than direct question estimate. I further investigate differences across measurement modes for relevant demographic and political subgroups and find no evidence in support of the 'Shy Trump Supporter' hypothesis."}

. . .

Present challenges in measuring Trump support more to do with non-response than social desirability.

Public opinion is often *thermostatic* -- moves in opposite direction of policy change

Democratic (blue) and Republican (red) administrations shown in background color shading. ## Regularities in Public Opinion{.smaller}

Depends on availability/use of information

::: {.incremental}

*   Media, well, *mediates* relationship between elites/public/policy
*   Relationship between political interest and attitude change?
    + Low interest: unlikely to encounter/less able to contextualize information
    + High interest: likelier to have strong predispositions/lots of prior information
    + Moderate interest: easiest to move

:::

## Wording Crimes

There's no such thing as a perfect question, but there is such a thing as a bad question.

Here are some things to avoid (among others)...

## Wording Crimes

Leading questions

Do you support or oppose replacing the final exam for Intro to American Politics with a less stressful, easier alternative?

*   Strongly support
*   Somewhat support
*   Neither support nor oppose
*   Somewhat oppose
*   Strongly oppose

## Wording Crimes

Jargon

Do you support or oppose including a question about linkage institutions on the final exam for Intro to American Politics?

*   Strongly support
*   Somewhat support
*   Neither support nor oppose
*   Somewhat oppose
*   Strongly oppose

## Wording Crimes

Imbalanced, incomplete, or indirect response options

Why did you enroll in Intro to American Politics? Check all that apply:

*   Because it fit my schedule
*   Because my friends enrolled
*   Because Professor Green is the best

## Wording Crimes

Too much cognitive load

Set reasonable expectations for respondents' memories

<br>

How many times have you raised your hand to speak in Intro to American Politics? 

Please enter a number:

## Wording Crimes

Too much cognitive load

Set reasonable expectations for how much respondents will read.

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="70%"}

::: {style="font-size: 35%;"}

Ungrading is a practice which eliminates or greatly minimizes the use of assigned points or letter grades in a course, focusing instead on providing frequent and detailed feedback to students on their work, in relation to the course learning goals. Ungrading is a form of “grading for growth,” in that the primary purpose of the assessment is to help students learn and improve their knowledge and skills, rather than to create a summative score that students use to compare themselves against an external credential.

Often, ungrading occurs in an educational environment in which a final letter grade *does* need to be assigned; in this case, typically the instructor (sometimes with input from or jointly with students) assigns a grade at the end of the course. In some courses the instructor will ask the students to self-assign a final, summative grade, using some specific guiding questions. The grade assigned may also be based on acceptable completion of work from a list of specifications, similar to contract or specifications grading.^[Text copied from https://learninginnovation.duke.edu/blog/2022/09/what-is-ungrading/]

Do you support ungrading Intro to American Politics?

*   Yes
*   No

:::

:::

::: {.column width="30%"}

![](images/happy_for_u.png){fig-alt="Meme: i aint reading all that. i'm happy for u tho. or sorry that happened."}

:::

::::

## Wording Crimes

Double-barreling

Do you support or oppose changing the time and location of Intro to American Politics?

*   Strongly support
*   Somewhat support
*   Neither support nor oppose
*   Somewhat oppose
*   Strongly oppose

## Wording Crimes

Asking people about their own causal effects

Does hearing that Professor Green teaches Campaigns and Elections make you more or less likely to enroll in the class?

*   More likely
*   Less likely
*   Neither more nor less likely

Divide into groups of 3-5. You're drafting our course evaluations.

Keep in mind:

*   Objective (what is important to measure?)
*   Audience (who will use this information for what?)
*   Clarity (put yourself in respondents' shoes)
*   Efficiency (tradeoffs between breadth and depth)

## Exit Quiz Answers {.smaller}

1.  Zaller's model of how individuals form political attitudes, and report those attitudes on surveys, includes four axioms. Name one.

. . .

1)  Reception: People who are more engaged are more likely to be exposed to and comprehend (i.e. receive) relevant messages.
2)  Resistance: People tend to resist messages that are inconsistent with their predispositions, but only if they understand the relationship between the message and their predispositions.
3)  Accessibility: Considerations that were brought to mind more recently are easier to retrieve.
4)  Response: The survey response is a weighted average of accessible considerations.

## Exit Quiz Answers

2.  Nate Cohn's article is entitled "How One Polling Decision is Leading to Two Distinct Stories of the Election." Name that decision.

. . .

Whether to include respondents’ recollection of who they voted for in 2020 in survey weights.

# Why Parties?

## Parties are fundamental to democracy

. . .

The framers warned us about parties, and yet...

. . .

Democracy is "a system where parties lose elections." - Adam Przeworski

Democracy is "unthinkable" without parties. - E.E. Schattschneider

. . .

Why?

## Why Parties?

Parties are an emergent property of democracy because [parties solve collective action problems]{.yellow}.

. . .

"...an organized attempt to get control of the government." (Schattschneider 1942)

## Why Parties?

Time for some game theory...

|         | Player A | Player B | Player C | Enacted? |
|---------|:--------:|:--------:|:--------:|:--------:|
| Issue 1 |    1     |    -1    |    0     |    No    |
| Issue 2 |    1     |    0     |    -1    |    No    |
| Issue 3 |    -1    |    1     |    0     |    No    |
| Issue 4 |    0     |    1     |    -1    |    No    |
| Issue 5 |    -1    |    0     |    1     |    No    |
| Issue 6 |    0     |    -1    |    1     |    No    |

. . .

No cooperation, no policy

## Why Parties?

Remember Federalist 10: cooperation is necessary

|                    |   Player A   |   Player B   | Player C |    Enacted?    |
|--------------------|:------------:|:------------:|:--------:|:--------------:|
| Issue 1            |      1       |      -1      |    0     |       No       |

| Issue 5            |      -1      |      0       |    1     |       No       |
| Issue 6            |      0       |      -1      |    1     |       No       |

Players A and B make a deal

## Why Parties?

Decision rule: if indifferent, defer to partner

|                  |  Player A  |  Player B  | Player C |   Enacted?   |
|------------------|:----------:|:----------:|:--------:|:------------:|
| Issue 1          |     1      |     -1     |    0     |      No      |
| [Issue 2]{.blue} | [1]{.blue} | [0]{.blue} |    -1    | [Yes]{.blue} |
| Issue 3          |     -1     |     1      |    0     |      No      |
| [Issue 4]{.blue} | [0]{.blue} | [1]{.blue} |    -1    | [Yes]{.blue} |

Players A and B form a [long coalition]{.yellow}

## Why Parties?

How does the coalition keep itself together?

. . .

In order to repeat their patterns of cooperation, coalitions need to be able to...

-   monitor members' behavior
-   reward cooperation
-   sanction defection

. . .

Parties develop the tools to do these things.

Who are Players A, B, and C here?

## Why Parties?

This is actually not settled in political science!

. . .

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Top-down view: parties are teams of politicians seeking to win elections

![](images/dnc.jpg){fig-alt="The Democratic National Convention 2020"}
:::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: fragment
Bottom-up view: parties are teams of "policy demanders" seeking to win policy

![](images/interest_groups.png){fig-alt="Interest group logos. From top-left to bottom-right: United Auto Workers, Sunrise, National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, United Farm Workers, Everytown for Gun Safety, National Education Association, Emily's List"}
:::

## Why Parties?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Top-down view: parties are teams of politicians seeking to win elections

![](images/dnc.jpg){fig-alt="The Democratic National Convention 2020 (pictures of Joe Biden and Kamala Harris)"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Middle-up view: parties are teams of "policy demanders" seeking to win policy

![](images/interest_groups.png){fig-alt="Interest group logos. From top-left to bottom-right: United Auto Workers, Sunrise, National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, United Farm Workers, Everytown for Gun Safety, National Education Association, Emily's List"}
:::
:::::

How do monitoring, rewarding, and sanctioning work in each of these models?

## Parties' Functions {.smaller}

What do parties *do* for democracy?

::: incremental
-   recruit, vet, nominate, and support candidates
-   develop policy proposals
-   help organize/staff government
-   structure issue space/debate
    -   formally in platforms, informally in stances/communication
    -   provide cues to voters re: "what goes with what"
:::

## Parties' Functions {.smaller}

Can restate these as collective actions

::: incremental
-   Coordination
    -   Manage conflicting ambitions/tradeoffs
    -   Set priorities
-   Public goods
    -   Party brand applies to all candidates
    -   Turning out one voter helps multiple candidates
-   Social choice
    -   Logrolling preferences breaks gridlock, stability clarifies alternatives
:::

## Party Brands

Parties become associated with sets of positions/ideas/groups over time

. . .

This brand can be useful for voters and politicians

::: incremental
-   voters: reduces costs of information search
-   politicians: reduces costs of educating voters on positions
:::

## Party Brands

But! Lower transaction costs mean higher conformity costs

Voters get "choice between compromises"

-   Many combinations of stances excluded
-   Many issues excluded

## Party Brands

Brands can serve as an accountability mechanism. [Why?]{.fragment}

. . .

Parties evaluated collectively, punished collectively for bad outcomes.

## Choice Between Compromises

U.S. has a two-party system. Why?

. . .

Implication: governing coalitions form *before* election, with voters choosing between them

::: fragment
-   (if you're frustrated with the two-party system, this is probably why)
:::

. . .

Multi-party system:

::: incremental
-   voters can express narrower preferences with their vote
-   if no majority, governing coalition forms *after* the election
:::

## U.S. Party Systems over Time {.smaller}

Can demarcate historical periods of stable two-party competition in the US as party "systems"

. . .

Five or six party systems, depending on where you draw the lines. General pattern:

-   Coalitions form around dominant cleavage
-   New cleavages threaten to split coalition arrangements
-   [Realignment]{.yellow} around new cleavage

. . .

Organizations often persist (institutional durability), but who and what they represent changes

. . .

Remember Duverger's Law. Single-member plurality elections a huge obstacle for minor parties.

## First Party System (1790s-1820s) {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Federalists

-   Urban/New England base
-   Merchant interests
-   Protective tariffs
-   Pro-national bank
-   Lean British

![](images/hamilton.jpeg){width="40%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Portrait of Alexander Hamilton"}
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
Democratic-Republicans

-   Rural/Southern base
-   Agricultural interests
-   Low tariffs
-   Anti-national bank
-   Lean French

![](images/jefferson.jpeg){width="50%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Portrait of Thomas Jefferson"}
:::
:::::

## First Party System (1790s-1820s) {.smaller}

Key developments:

-   Primarily legislative (small electorate)
-   Era of Good Feelings
    -   Democratic-Republican dominance (Monroe essentially unopposed for re-election)
-   First (disorganized) groups
    -   Informal nomination procedures
    -   Candidates promoted through clubs, newsletters, informal networks

## Second Party System (1830s-1856) {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Democrats

-   Continuation of Democratic-Republicans
-   Populist
-   Pro-slavery

![](images/andrew_jackson.jpg){width="45%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Portrait of Andrew Jackson"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Whigs

-   Opposition party
-   Urban/educated
-   Split on slavery

![](images/henry_clay.jpeg){width="50%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Portrait of Henry Clay"}
:::
:::::

## Second Party System (1830s-1856) {.smaller}

Key developments:

-   Expansion of electorate (removal of property requirements)
    -   Extension of competition for new voters
-   Development of party organizations/newspaper networks
    -   First party conventions
-   Spoils system
-   Suppression of slavery as potential cleavage

## Third Party System (1857-1896) {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Democrats

-   Pro-slavery/anti-Reconstruction
-   Southern + urban bases
    -   Machines assimilate immigrants, urban workers

![](images/tweed.jpeg){width="50%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Picture of Boss Tweed"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Republicans

-   Anti-slavery
-   Northeastern base
-   Pro-business

![](images/lincoln.jpeg){fig-alt="Picture of Abraham Lincoln"}
:::
:::::

## Third Party System (1857-1896)

Key developments

-   Civil War -\> Reconstruction -\> Jim Crow
-   Industrial Revolution / Gilded Age
    -   Clarification of economic cleavage
-   Development of political machines in cities
    -   "Honest graft" analogous to previous spoils system
    -   Parties as central features of *social* life

## Fourth Party System (1897-1932) {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Democrats

-   Southern + industrial base
    -   White primary, de-facto one-party rule in South
-   Anti-immigration

![](images/wilson.png){width="50%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Picture of Woodrow Wilson"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Republicans

-   Non-Southern, middle-class base
-   Pro-business
-   Less anti-immigration

![](images/roosevelt.jpeg){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Picture of Teddy Roosevelt"}
:::
:::::

## Fourth Party System (1897-1932) {.smaller}

Key developments

-   Government takes over party functions / weakens parties
    -   Secret ballot (states adopted between 1884-1891)
    -   Administration of elections
    -   Social services
-   Progressive Era reforms
    -   Women's suffrage
    -   Civil service reform
    -   Direct primary and senate elections
-   Emergence/incorporation of minor parties (Progressives, Populists)

## Fifth Party System (1933-1968) {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Democrats

-   New Deal coalition
    -   Working class base
    -   Racial realignment / "Dixiecrats"
-   More active government in economy

![](images/RooseveltNewDeal.jpg){width="50%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="FDR campaign button, slogan 'For A New Deal'"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Republicans

-   (Mostly) opposition party
-   Middle class base
-   Pro-business
    -   Opposed New Deal spending/regulation
    -   More anti-communist

![](images/eisenhower.jpg){width="50%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Picture of Dwight Eisenhower"}
:::
:::::

## Fifth Party System (1933-1968) {.smaller}

Key developments

-   Great Depression
-   World War II --\> Cold War
-   Civil Rights Movement
-   Racial realignment
    -   Starts early, takes time (we'll come back to this)
-   Weaker parties --\> candidate-centered elections

## Quick Aside

1950: American Political Science Association report on political parties

. . .

Key argument: parties *aren't polarized enough*, voters need clearer choice

. . .

Now seems like a product of being in the middle of long-term sorting

## 1968 {.smaller}

Chain of events lead to democratization of parties' nomination procedures

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
::: incremental
-   Robert F. Kennedy (JFK's brother, RFK Jr's father) assassinated after winning CA primary
    -   Had been running on anti-war platform
-   Humphrey nominated at convention over McGovern
    -   Hadn't campaigned in primaries
    -   Not anti-war
-   Protests turned to riots at the convention
:::
::::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/rfk.png){fig-alt="Robert F. Kennedy (senior) speaking to supporters in Los Angeles prior to being assassinated."}
:::
::::::

## 1968's Aftermath {.smaller}

McGovern-Fraser Commission convenes to amend rules in response

-   "The cure for the ills of democracy is more democracy."
-   Changes to Democratic delegate selection procedures (incl. pledged delegates)
    -   Republicans soon followed suit
    -   More states shifted to selecting delegates in primaries (vs. caucuses/conventions)

. . .

McGovern, not entirely coincidentally, wins nomination in 1972 (and loses badly in the general)

## Sixth Party System (1969-present) {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Democrats

-   More active government in economy
-   Culturally liberal
-   More dovish foreign policy
-   Urban base

![](images/obama.png){width="40%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Picture of Barack Obama"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Republicans

-   Less active government in economy
-   Culturally conservative
-   More hawkish foreign policy
-   Rural base

![](images/reagan.jpeg){width="40%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Picture of Ronald Reagan"}
:::
:::::

## Sixth Party System (1969-present) {.smaller}

Key developments

-   Nationalization of politics
    -   Harder to develop distinct/local brands
-   "Conflict extension" (Layman and Carsey 2002)
    -   Polarization
    -   Sorting

Foiled by Duverger. But! Can influence major party agendas or sub-national government.

Present

# Where's the Party?

## Where are parties located?

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="70%"}
A few different places!

::: incremental
-   Party in government
    -   Elected officials, appointed bureaucrats
-   Party in organization
    -   Campaign committees
-   Party in the electorate
    -   Voters, activists
:::
::::

::: {.column width="30%"}
![V.O. Key](images/vokey.png){fig-alt="Picture of V.O. Key"}
:::

## Party in Government

. . .

Question: is Bernie Sanders a Democrat?

. . .

POLSCI 242: Campaigns and Elections

## Why elections? {.smaller}

What are elections...for?

::: incremental
-   Basic premise of "rule by many"
-   Non-violent mechanism for conferring authority
-   Sanction representatives to exercise accountability
    -   [Retrospective]{.yellow} evaluations
-   Select representatives to shape policy
    -   [Prospective]{.yellow} evaluations
    -   If hard to monitor for accountability, try to select faithful agent
:::

## Before we dive in...

It is *extremely strange* that President Trump was allowed to run for office post-Jan 6.

-   Failure of elite gatekeeping (Senate, SCOTUS, Republican Party)

. . .

We only get to disagree about policy if we agree about democracy ("a system where parties lose elections")

. . .

Prisoner's dilemma: must be more costly for losing incumbent to defect (reject election results) than to cooperate (accept election results)

## Election mechanics {.smaller}

Administering an election involves answering these questions (among others)...

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Basics:

-   Who can run?
    -   Age/residency requirements?
-   Who can vote?
    -   Eligibility requirements?
    -   Registration requirements?
        -   Closed primary, e.g.?
-   Who's on the ballot?
    -   Candidates? Party lists?
-   How to vote?
    -   Where? When?
    -   How many votes on a single ballot?
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Decision rules:

-   How to count?
    -   Single/multiple/ranked choice?
        -   How to allocate ranked choices?
    -   When to recount?
-   How is a winner determined?
    -   How many winners are there?
        -   Single/multi-member?
    -   Plurality? Majority? Proportional?
:::
:::::

## How to vote

States have wide latitude to set administrative procedures

::: incremental
-   Typically require registration
    -   Many states offer some form of same-day registration
    -   ND abolished voter registration in 1951
-   Vary in extent of absentee/early/mail-in voting
    -   Some states (Oregon, e.g.) fully by mail
    -   Absentee vs. early: absentee typically requires reason
:::

## When is the election? {.smaller}

Election Day is the Tuesday after the first Monday in November (since 1845)

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
Goes back to making voting convenient for farmers

::: incremental
-   Sunday (church) and Wednesday (market day) unavailable for travel, also ruling out Monday and Thursday
    -   Tuesday
-   After harvest season, but before it gets too cold
    -   Early November
-   November 1 ruled out (All Saints Day)
:::
::::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/snl_when.png){fig-alt="Screenshot of SNL sketch with an undecided voter asking, 'When is the election?'"}
:::
::::::

. . .

Path dependence!

## Presidential election mechanics {.smaller}

Really 51 (including DC) state elections with some common features

-   Who can run?
    -   35yr+ natural-born citizen
-   Who can vote?
    -   18yr+ citizens (with some exclusions)
-   How do they vote?
    -   Varies by state
-   How do ballots get counted?
    -   Varies by state
-   How is a winner determined?
    -   Majority in Electoral College
        -   If no EC majority, House delegations vote

Why do people vote?

::: incremental
-   resources
-   habits
-   social context (norms, networks)
-   competition
-   candidate/issue preferences
-   campaign contact
:::

## Big Picture (Participation)

Why do people vote?

. . .

Economic model: U = pB - C + D

::: incremental
-   [U]{.yellow}: utility of voting (vote if \> 0)
-   [p]{.yellow}: probability your vote is decisive
-   [B]{.yellow}: net benefits from your preferred candidate winning
-   [C]{.yellow}: costs of voting
-   [D]{.yellow}: intrinsic benefits of voting (regardless of who wins)
:::

## Big Picture (Participation)

Why do people vote?

Economic model: U = pB - C + D

The economic model is pretty vague. Can we unpack it? What goes under which term?

## Big Picture (Participation)

Why do people vote?

Economic model: U = pB - C + D

Common to drop pB

::: incremental
-   p is \~0, so pB is \~0
-   U = D - C?
    -   Puzzle: \~nobody votes because they think the outcome matters to them?
:::

## Big Picture (Participation) {.smaller}

Some objections to dropping pB in practice:

::: incremental
-   p is small but not zero...and B is large
-   p is subjective (can be overestimated)
-   p is endogenous (those who prefer to believe their vote matters behave as if it does)
-   uncertainty about what others will do
    -   if everybody behaves as if their vote doesn't matter, your vote is decisive *by definition*!
-   voting is a collective action sustained by norms
    -   p is probability that *people like you* are decisive
:::

## Big Picture (Choice): Spatial Models

General explanation for spatial clustering (fast food chains, gas stations, e.g.)

. . .

Downs (1957) restates as [Median Voter Theorem]{.yellow}

-   Not meant to fully explain politics, but useful jumping off point

## Big Picture (Choice): Spatial Models

More concretely, worth thinking about [how candidates/parties appeal to pivotal voters]{.yellow}.

. . .

Spatial proximity is one explanation. [Debate over whether what matters is proximity per se, vs. *direction* of expected change.]{.fragment}

## Big Picture (Choice) {.smaller}

Assumptions that make the hot dog equilibrium (and Median Voter Theorem) work:

::: incremental
-   [one dimension]{.yellow}: beach, not mall; no one's selling ice cream
-   [exogenous preferences]{.yellow}: beach umbrellas stay in same spot regardless of where vendors move
-   [full participation]{.yellow}: everyone buys a hot dog no matter how far they have to walk
-   [complete information]{.yellow}: everyone sees/agrees where vendors and consumers are
-   [no uncertainty]{.yellow}: vendor isn't trying to convince you of where they'll set up shop tomorrow
-   [unitary actor]{.yellow}: consumers on edge of the beach aren't part of the business
-   [free movement]{.yellow}: no lags or competing claims over perceived (re)positioning
:::

. . .

Useful for thinking about *when and how these assumptions are (not) met*.

## Big Picture (Choice): Behavior {.smaller}

Second model: partisanship serves as default setting/"standing decision," additional factors may lead voters to change behavior

Worth considering...what factors affect vote choice? [In rough temporal order...]{.fragment}

::: incremental
-   (pre)dispositions
-   socialization (family and friends)
-   salient identities (race, gender, age, religion)
-   partisanship/ideology
-   specific issues
-   valence (non-ideological candidate traits)
-   material conditions (sociotropic)
-   material conditions (personal)
-   current events
:::

. . .

Can interact; earlier factors can affect evaluation of later factors.

First two models are *prospective*; third is *retrospective*.

Voters observe events, actions, and outcomes in incumbent's term --> Attribute credit/blame for those events, actions, and outcomes --> Evaluate incumbent, vote --> Elected officials respond to electoral incentives --> Voters observe events, actions, and outcomes in incumbent's term"}

## Big Picture (Choice): Psychology {.smaller}

Psychological factors:

::: incremental
-   Heuristics (partisanship, e.g.) affect evaluations
-   Recency bias (more weight on recent performance)
-   Myopia
    -   More credit for (costlier, more visible) response than (cheaper, less visible) prevention
-   "Blind" retrospection (credit/blame for irrelevant events)
    -   Unexpected college football results, e.g.
:::

. . .

These aren't all *bad*. [Heuristics are *useful*; more recent information might *warrant* higher weight; voters use relevant information *when they have it*, e.g.]{.fragment.}

Fundamentals models make vote share fairly predictable (outcomes hard to predict lately because vote share was predictably close)

Post-COVID unwinding has led voters to penalize incumbents pretty much everywhere

## Campaign Effects {.smaller}

So (when/why) do campaigns matter?

. . .

Strategic campaigns tailor strategy to economic conditions (Vavreck 2009):

::: incremental
-   Clarifying campaign: party advantaged by economic fundamentals emphasizes them
-   Insurgent campaign: party disadvantaged by economic fundamentals emphasizes other issues where
    -   that party's positions popular/that party owns issue
    -   other party's positions are unpopular/lacks ownership
:::

. . .

Two high-profile, well-resourced general election campaigns often cancel each other out. Doesn't mean they don't matter.

. . .

Effects easier to observe in primaries and open-seat races (no partisan cue, less baked-in familiarity)

## Campaign Effects {.smaller}

Campaigns still serve important functions:

::: incremental
-   information
    -   help voters learn about economic conditions
    -   reinforce existing views/bring partisans home
-   salience
    -   contest which cleavage will be dominant
-   valence
    -   make claims on efficacy/trustworthiness
-   mobilization
    -   encourage supporters to participate
:::

## Winning Coalitions

Getting to your "win number" means thinking about [marginal voters]{.yellow}. Two types of marginal voter:

::: incremental
-   Might vote, will vote for you if they do
    -   Mobilization
-   Will vote, might vote for you
    -   Persuasion
:::

. . .

If you don't fall into either of these groups, campaign messaging *is not for you* (volunteer/donation appeals separate).

## Winning Coalitions

To what extent do mobilization and persuasion trade off against each other?

## Winning Coalitions

Let's talk about this for a second.

"Persuasion" as we commonly understand the term (and as some of you learned last week) is *really hard*.

. . .

But, campaigns can persuade people to vote for them *without changing their minds*.

## The Art of Manipulation

Campaigns manipulate[^1] the political terrain using [heresthetics]{.yellow} (Riker 1986)

[^1]: non-derogatory

. . .

Rhetoric: winning the debate at hand

Heresthetic: altering terms of debate to be more favorable

. . .

Vavreck's "insurgent campaigns" rely on heresthetics.

. . .

Aim is to set agenda on issue that divides your opponent's coalition and unites yours.

## Campaign Messages

Campaigns develop a "message box"

|            |    We Say    |  They Say  |
|------------|:------------:|:----------:|
| About Us   |    Why us    | Why not us |
| About Them | Why not them |  Why them  |

. . .

Decisions early on about what you want the race to be "about"

. . .

Campaign rhetoric is repetitive by design.

## Ads

Ads can be...

-   positive: why you're good
-   negative: why they're bad
-   inoculating: why you aren't bad
-   contrasting: why you're better

## Ads

People say they don't like negative ads, and yet we see a lot of them. Why?

. . .

Negative ads are often *informative*

![](images/negative_katko.jpeg){width="70%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Image from a negative ad against Rep. John Katko, featuring a headline from syracues.com reading 'Why Central New York's biggest Obamacare insurer wants whopping 39 percent rate hike' with the text: 'John Katko's vote: Jacking up insurance premiums 39%'"}

## Ads

People say they don't like negative ads, and yet we see a lot of them. Why?

Candidates in a prisoner's dilemma

|   | Candidate B Positive | Candidate B Negative |
|----|:--:|:--:|
| Candidate A Positive | Competitive, reputations intact | B wins |
| Candidate A Negative | A wins | Competitive, reputations harmed |

## Ads

It's hard to know what messages will be effective without pre-testing.

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/shor_ads.png){fig-alt="Headline of an article by David Shor: With message testing, popularity does not equal persuasiveness"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/shor_ads_context.png){fig-alt="Text from the article: 'We saw this first-hand when working on the Doug Jones campaign in Alabama last December. Opponent Roy Moore was mired in controversy and scandal, so it seemed intuitive to focus Jones ads on Moore's reported misconduct. But when we tested the messaging, we found that ads emphasizing Jones's ability to improve education in the state were in fact the most persuasive. While people might have responded favorably to ads focused on the Moore scandal, the media had publicized it enough that additional messaging didn't actually *change minds*. Interestingly, we also found that messages aligning Moore with Trump didn't persuade voters to support Jones -- rather, it dissuaded certain groups to vote at all.'"}
:::
:::::

## Ground Game

Direct voter contact about *winning the margins*

-   Canvassing
-   Phonebanking/textbanking
-   Relational organizing (contact through personal networks)

. . .

Phases:

-   ID likely/potential supporters
-   Persuade undecideds
-   Mobilize confirmed supporters (GOTV)

## Money

Money obviously matters, but people often overestimate *how much* and *where* it matters.

. . .

Difficult to identify:

-   Campaign contributions affecting roll call votes
    -   Any given contribution is small share of total, issue priority unclear
    -   Easier to help an ally than win a convert
-   How many dollars to buy a vote
    -   Closest races see highest spending

## Campaign Finance

Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 (FECA): first *comprehensive* campaign finance regulations

-   Disclosure requirements
-   Partial public funding
-   Federal Elections Commission

. . .

Spending limits struck down in *Buckley v. Valeo (1976)*, which set initial precedent that (spending) money is speech.

## Campaign Finance {.smaller}

Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002 (aka McCain-Feingold)

-   Designed to regulate "soft money" (i.e. money not directly contributed to campaigns)
    -   Contribution limits
        -   Generally upheld by SCOTUS (interest in anti-corruption warrants limiting speech)
        -   Limits on aggregate contribution across all committees overturned
    -   Restrictions on issue ads near elections
        -   Overturned by SCOTUS
    -   Restrictions on self-financing
        -   Overturned by SCOTUS
    -   Restrictions on election communication from corporations/unions
        -   Overturned by SCOTUS (*Citizens United*)

## Campaign Finance

General theme: government's interest in regulating campaign finance is about *preventing corruption*, not *equal voice*

. . .

*Value conflict* between freedom (of speech) and equality (of voice) when some can "speak" louder than others.

## Political Action Committees {.smaller}

Emerged in response to restrictions on who could directly contribute

-   CIO-PAC in 1943

. . .

"Connected" PACs: political arms of established organizations (non-connected PACs for issues, candidates, e.g.)

. . .

Leadership PACs: non-connected PACs for elected officials

-   Can make independent expenditures as long they aren't coordinated with/directly for member's own campaign (can distribute to other members' campaigns, e.g.)

## Super PACs

Not subject to contribution or spending limits, so long as they are fully independent.

. . .

-   No coordination with/donations to campaigns
-   Same disclosure requirements as regular PACs, but...
    -   Intermediaries can circumvent disclosure
    -   Quarterly filing --\> final push disclosed after the election

Super PACs change campaign dynamics.

## Exit Quiz Answers

1.  In Vavreck's model of campaign effects, campaigns engage in three core behaviors. Name one.

::: incremental
-   Agenda setting: refocusing the voters’ attention to issues favorable to the candidate/changing the weights voters place on certain issues
-   Persuading: convincing voters that candidates hold particular positions on specific issues
-   Clarifying: educating voters about their positions on already-important issues
:::

## Exit Quiz Answers {.smaller}

2.  (2 pts, second is bonus) Grimmer/Marble and Sides/Tesler/Vavreck offer different accounts of why Donald Trump won in 2016, but Lynn Vavreck in particular argues that the two teams are really answering different questions about the 2016 election. What are these two questions?

::: incremental
-   Sides/Tesler/Vavreck: Change in relationship between racial attitudes and vote choice among voters?
-   Grimmer/Marble: Change in contribution of racially \[moderate/conservative\] voting blocs to Republican coalition?
    -   i.e. change in composition of the electorate, accounting for turnout
:::

## This week

Interest Groups

## Interest Groups

What do we already know about interest groups?

::: incremental
-   Related to factions/policy demanders
    -   Worth thinking about where the lines are
-   Interact with...
    -   Members of Congress
    -   Executive branch / bureaucracy
    -   Parties
:::

## Stated formally

An interest group is an [organization]{.yellow} whose members [share preferences]{.yellow} and attempt to [influence policy]{.yellow} through [electioneering and lobbying]{.yellow}.

## Logic of Lobbying

::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="70%"}
Politics is our process for determining who gets what.

::: fragment
Interest groups form when individuals act collectively to try and get what they want.
:::

::: fragment
Political scientists' pet peeve: "special" interest groups just means *other people's* interest groups.
:::
:::::

::: {.column width="30%"}
![](images/chamber_of_commerce.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="The logo for the United States Chamber of Commerce"}
:::
:::::::

## Linkage Institutions

Interest groups are [linkage institutions]{.yellow}: a mechanism that connects citizens to policymakers / provides a channel for communicating preferences.

. . .

Elections, parties, and the media are also linkage institutions.

. . .

Interest group signals as (difficult to quantify) public opinion?

## Interest Group Pluralism

Early theory of interest groups: pluralism

. . .

Diverse array of interests organize and *compete* for power

. . .

Diversity of interests is balancing, no one group can become too powerful

## Pluralism's Critics

What's missing here?

::: incremental
-   Uneven playing field
    -   strength in dollars
-   Logic of collective action
    -   easier to organize some interests than others (debt reduction, e.g.)
    -   some groups better-able to overcome free-rider problems
-   If broader public doesn't provide input, is that tacit agreement?
:::

## Promoting collective action

What can interest groups do to discourage free riding?

::: incremental
-   Moral incentives
    -   Public interest sign-ups, e.g.
-   Selective benefits
    -   AAA, e.g.
-   Compulsory participation
    -   Labor unions, e.g.
:::

## Why Join?

Different types of benefits

. . .

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
More outcome-based:

::: incremental
-   [Material]{.yellow}: tangible benefits (may be specific to group membership)
-   [Purposive]{.yellow}: benefits from working to achieve a broader policy goal (skills, e.g.)
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
Less outcome-based:

::: incremental
-   [Solidary]{.yellow}: benefits from working together (community, friendship, e.g.)
-   [Expressive]{.yellow}: benefits from signaling group membership
:::
::::
:::::::

## Interest Group Mechanics

Interest groups may vary in how much direct input their members have.

. . .

AARP, e.g. -- selective benefits for members, but members don't direct lobbying priorities

![](images/aarp.jpeg){width="60%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="The logo for the AARP"}

## Lobbying in the Public Interest

Public interest lobbies...examples?

. . .

-   Consumer advocacy
-   Environmentalism
-   Anti-homelessness

. . .

What do these have in common?

. . .

Organizers overlap with but not necessarily beneficiaries

. . .

Heavily reliant on [moral incentives]{.yellow} ("help us help others")

## Expansion of Interest Groups

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="60%"}
Size, scope, and nature of interest group activity interacts with technology and political landscape

::: fragment
Earlier bottom-up [voluntary associations]{.yellow} largely gave way to top-down [advocacy organizations]{.yellow}
:::
::::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/voluntary_association.jpeg){fig-alt="Picture of a crowded meeting room for a voluntary association"}
:::
::::::

## Expansion of Interest Groups

Interest group activity more concentrated in DC now than in previous eras

. . .

Linked to expansion in size/scope of federal government, but which way does causal arrow go?

-   Larger federal government --\> more interest group organization
-   More interest group organization --\> larger federal government

## Interest group activities

Think about your own experience with interest groups.

::: incremental
-   How often are you asked to sign petitions?
    -   Or put your name on an email list?
-   How often are you asked to donate money?
-   How often are you asked to attend a meeting?
:::

## Market of Influence {.smaller}

::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="60%"}
Lobbying is a regulated business.

::: incremental
-   Quarterly reporting of how much which clients spent on which issues
-   Reporting requirements for interest groups/corporations' lobbying activity
-   Requirement to register if acting on behalf of foreign government
:::

::: fragment
Relatively light restrictions on "revolving door" from government staff to lobbying.

-   Typically one-year cooling off for staff / two years for electeds
:::
:::::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/k_street.png){fig-alt="Street sign at the 1500 block of K Street NW in Washington, DC"}
:::
:::::::

## Market of Influence {.smaller}

Lobbying is a big business because *the stakes are really high*

. . .

-   Total federal outlays in 2024: 6.8 trillion
-   Total spending on federal lobbying in 2024: \$4.5 billion (.066% of outlays)

. . .

Top spenders tend to represent industries with heavy government involvement

-   Chamber of Commerce
-   National Association of Realtors
-   Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America
-   American Hospital Association

## How Lobbying Matters

Intuitive to think that lobbying systematically buys politicians' support, but this is often difficult to quantify. Why?

. . .

Easier to help an ally than win a convert

-   Lobbying as [legislative subsidy]{.yellow}: providing information, expertise, and political support to help politicians draft/prioritize legislation that they already want to pass

## How Lobbying Matters

Doesn't mean lobbying never secures initial support, especially when politician begins indifferent

. . .

And, money in other places can help allies win elections in the first place

. . .

But! It does mean that "politicians are bought and paid for" is a bit too simple

## How Lobbying Matters

Less professionalized legislatures rely more heavily on lobbyists.

Tradeoff relevant to debates over congressional staffing and term limits:

-   High turnover in Congress --\> more reliance on/deference to lobbyists

## Market of Influence

Who works for interest groups?

::: incremental
-   Policy experts ("wonks")
-   Politics experts ("hacks")
:::

## Market of Influence

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="40%"}
Interest group representatives often hired back into government agencies.

::: fragment
This often looks unseemly...why haven't we banned it?
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="60%"}
![](images/sec_clayton.png){fig-alt="Open Secrets page for former Securities and Exchange Commissioner Jay Clayton, who worked at the lobbying firm Sullivan & Cromwell for over 20 years before being appointed SEC chairman."}

::: {style="font-size: 50%;"}
https://www.opensecrets.org/revolving/rev_summary.php?id=79303
:::
::::
:::::::

## Interest Groups and Social Movements {.smaller}

What's the difference?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Social movements

-   Loosely organized
-   Lobbying *public* to think/care about issue
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Interest groups

-   Formally organized
-   Lobbying *government* for specific policy
:::
:::::

Both demonstrate *power* and encourage responsiveness to policy demands.

. . .

Lines can blur / overlap. Interest groups can grow out of social movements.

## Tactics {.smaller}

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
Insider:

::: incremental
-   Interact with government
    -   legislature
        -   members and staff
    -   bureaucracy
-   Testimony, meetings, calls, emails, comments on regulations, etc.
-   Repeated game, important to stay credible
    -   On both substance and politics
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
Outsider:

::: incremental
-   Pressuring government
    -   From petitioning to protesting to advertising
-   Aim to alter incentives
:::
::::
:::::::

## NAACP / CIO

![](images/baylor_abstract.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Title page for Baylor (2013). Title: First to the Party: The Group Origins of the Partisan Transformation on Civil Rights, 1940-1960. Author: Christopher A. Baylor, College of the Holy Cross. Abstract: One of the most momentous shifts in twentieth-century party politics was the Democratic Party's embrace of civil rights. Recent scholarship finds that this realignment began as early as the 1940s and traces it to pressure groups, especially organized labor. But such scholarship does not explain why labor, which was traditionally hostile to African Americans, began to work with them. Nor does it ascribe agency to the efforts of African American pressure groups. Focusing on the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) and the Congress of Industrial Organizations (CIO), this article attempts to fill these gaps in the literature. It explains why civil rights and labor leaders reassessed their traditional animosities and began to work as allies in the Democratic Party. It further shows how pressure from the new black-blue alliance forced the national Democratic Party to stop straddling civil rights issues and to become instead the vehicle for promoting civil rights. NAACP and CIO leaders consciously sought to remake the Democratic Party by marginalizing conservative Southerners, and eventually succeeded."}

## NAACP / CIO {.smaller}

NAACP's internal politics: Walter White (not that one) vs. W.E.B. Du Bois

. . .

Being a "team player" means taking short-term losses (like slow-walking civil rights provisions of labor laws) for long-term gains

. . .

Compatible --\> coherent

. . .

Heading off the "demands of those who seek to push us into third party adventures"

. . .

The Fair Employment Practices Commission (FEPC) as a wedge issue

. . .

Coalition politics in nominations and platforms

. . .

NAACP starts as junior partner, ends as peer?

## NRA

The puzzle:

![](images/polls_background_checks.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Morning Consult article. Headline: Voters are Nearly United in Support for Expanded Background Checks. Subhed: But electorate is more divided on legislation aimed at closing 'Charleston loophole'. Author: Eli Yokley. Date: March 10, 2021. Key Takeaways: 84% of voters, including 77% of Republicans, support requiring all gun purchasers to go through a background check. 48% support closing the 'Charleston loophole', while 38% oppose the move. Voter are more likely to trust Democrats than Republicans on gun policy, 44% to 38%, though it's an area of relative weakness for the president's party."}

## NRA

Common answers:

::: incremental
-   Issue importance
    -   Minority votes on issue; majority doesn't
        -   But! This might be changing
-   Money
    -   Not obvious that funding is unequal for/against
:::

## NRA

Emerging answer: "people who own guns" --\> "gun owners"

![](images/lacombe_nra.png){fig-alt="Journal article title page. Title: The Political Weaponization of Gun Owners: The National Rifle Association's Cultivation, Dissemination, and Use of a Group Social Identity. Author: Matthew J. Lacombe, Barnard College, Columbia University. Abstract: There is substantial evidence indicating that the NRA's (National Rifle Association) political influence is closely tied to the deep political engagement of the minority of Americans who oppose strict gun control laws. This explanation of the NRA’s influence, however, raises its own questions; namely, why are gun owners so devoted to their cause, and why is the NRA so effective at mobilizing them? I marshal a wide range of evidence covering nearly nine decades to demonstrate that an important cause of the political activity of gun owners is the NRA’s long-term cultivation and dissemination of a distinct, politicized gun owner social identity, which the NRA uses to mobilize mass political action on its behalf. My findings shed new light on the ability of interest groups to develop and use resources that help them influence policy by altering the political behavior of members of the mass public."}

## NRA

Hahrie Han has some pretty tough words for gun control groups. What did you think?
