## Let's talk about milk

What *is* milk?

![](images/got_milk.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="got milk? logo"}

## So here's the issue

::::: columns
::: {.column width="70%"}
![https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfcfr/cfrsearch.cfm?fr=131.110](images/fda_milk.png){fig-alt="Code of Federal Regulations Title 21 -- Food and Drugs, Chapter I -- Food and Drug Administration Department of Health and Human Services, Subchapter B -- Food for Human Consumption, Part 131 -- Milk and Cream, Subpart B -- Requirements for Specific Standardized Milk and Cream, Section 131.110: Milk. (a) Description. Milk is the lacteal secretion, practically free from colostrum, obtained by the complete milking of one or more healthy cows. Milk that is in final package form for beverage use shall have been pasteurized or ultrapasteurized, and shall contain not less than 8 1/4 pecent milk solids not fat and not less than 3 1/4 percent milkfat. Milk may have been adjusted by separating part of the milkfat therefrom, or by adding thereto cream, concentrated milk, dry whole milk, skim milk, concentrated skim milk, or nonfat dry milk. Milk may be homogenized."}
:::

::: {.column width="30%"}
![](images/oatly.png){fig-alt="A box of Oatly oat milk"}
:::
:::::

## Your job {.smaller}

Divide into groups of three. Each group will be given an interest to represent.

. . .

Your group's job is to:

-   Consider the proposed rule
-   Draft a public comment [from your interest's perspective]{.yellow}
    -   What should the FDA do about plant-based milk labeling?
        -   Is the proposed rule acceptable? If not, what should they change?
    -   [Why]{.yellow} should the FDA adopt your group's preferred policy?
-   Don't worry about writing this down, we'll talk it out

. . .

You may review the public comments that were actually submitted here: https://www.regulations.gov/document/FDA-2023-D-0451-0002/comment

-   If you don't want to type out the URL, to the regulations.gov home page, search for docket ID [FDA-2023-D-0451-0002]{.yellow}, and click on "Browse Posted Comments"

## Your job {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
The proposed rule (FDA Docket Number FDA-2023-D-0451):

-   Plant-based milk can be marketed as "milk" as long as it identifies plant source
    -   "oat milk" is fine; "imitation milk" is typically not necessary
-   Plant-based milk producers are encouraged to voluntarily include nutritional differences from cow's milk
    -   Specifically (but not limited to) calcium, protein, vitamins A/D/B12, magnesium, phosphorous, potassium, or riboflavin
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![Example](images/milk_labeling_fda.png){fig-alt="Example from the proposed rule. Figure 1: Example of Voluntary Nutrient Statement on Product Label netxt to Product Name (box includes in small print next to product name: Contains a lower amount of potassium than milk). Figure 2: Example of Voluntary Nutrient Statement on Product Label next to Product Name: (same disclaimer, but zoomed in)"}
:::
:::::

## How this played out

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/milk_quote.png){fig-alt="Excerpt from article covering the proposed rule: 'Woefully insufficient'. The National Milk PRoducers Federation (NMPF) said the FDA proposal 'falls woefully short of ending the decades-old problem of misleading plant-based labeling using dairy terminology but supported the federal agency's initiative to introduce nutrient statements, designed to highlight any significant nutritional differences between dairy milk and a plant-based alternative. 'For far too long, plant-based beverage manufacturers have blurred well-defined standards of identity to inappropriately and unfairly capitalize on dairy's nutritional benefits while FDA has ignored its enforcement obligations,' said Jim Mulhern, NMPF president and CEO. 'FDA's draft guidance is an encouraging first step toward promoting labeling transparency in the marketplace, but it's not enough. Our comments outline a solution to the misleading labeling practices existing in the marketplace today, and provide clear, truthful labeling options for marketers of plant-based beverages."}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/vege_quote.png){fig-alt="Another excerpt: 'No justification for an uprecedecnted, unique, disparaging disclaimer' Proponents in favor of the use of dairy terms on dairy alternative products argued adopting 'milk' for use on plant-based products would be in line with what consumers were accustomed to. In its comments to the FDA, the Vegetarian Resource Groups -- an NGO dedicated to promoting vegetarianism -- said results of a survey it commissioned in 2020 suggested that 92% of US adults 'recognized that soy milk and dairy milk were different.' 'This supports our view that use of 'milk' to describe a plant-baed milk will not be confusing to consumers.'"}

![](images/vege_quote_2.png){fig-alt="Another excerpt: The Plant Based Foods Association, a trade body that represents plant-based food companies, had submitted a 19-page statement in which it rebukes the need for nutrient disclaimers, questions the FDA's proposed use of the school nutrition standards that plant-based alternatives must meet, and suggests that the FDA had relied on 'questionable research and empirical evidence' that informed its recommendation for voluntary nutrient statements and naming obligations. The trade body argued that 'there is no justification for an unprecedented, unique, disparaging disclaimer' highlighting that plant-based products were low in nutrients that were not of public health concern, such as magnesium or protein. Of the nine essential nutrients contained in milk, only calcium, vitamin D, and potassium have been identified as such within the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, yet the FDA recommends manufacturers to highlight nutritional differences related to magnesium or protein content, the body said."}
:::
:::::

::: {style="font-size: 50%;"}
Lyubomirova, Teodora. "Dairy and plant-based organizations go head-to-head over FDA’s plant-based milk labeling guidance." Dairy Reporter, August 3, 2023.
:::

## How this played out

End result: plant-based milk can be marketed as milk.

-   Producers encouraged, but not required, to note nutritional differences from dairy

. . .

But!

![](images/dairy_pride.png){width="60%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="Press release from Senator Tammy Baldwin: Baldwin, Risch, Collins, Welch, Introduce Bipartisan DAIRY PRIDE Act to Combat Mislabeling of Non-Dairy Products. Washington, DC -- Following the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's proposed guidance last week allowingnut, oat, soy, and other non-dairy products to use the name 'milk,' Senators Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), Jim Risch (R-ID), Susan Collins (R-ME), and Peter Welch (D-VT) today introduced bipartisan legislation to combat the unfair practice of mislabeling non-dairy products using dairy names. The Defending Against Imitations and Replacements of Yogurt, milk, and cheese to Promote Regular Intake of Dairy Everyday Act (DAIRY PRIDE Act) of 2023 would require non-dairy products made from nuts, seeds, plants, and algae to no longer be mislabeled with dairy terms such as milk, yogurt, or cheese."}

## Some premises: information

Information is the raw materials of democracy.

. . .

Individuals need information to understand their interests and contribute to collective decisions

::: incremental
-   We'd like that information to be reliable
-   We'd like more information rather than less
    -   More *types* (local vs. national)
    -   More *sources* (competition, corroboration)
    -   More *perspectives* (the better to aggregate)
-   We'd like to prioritize more vs. less important information
:::

## Some premises: transaction costs

On our own, being informed has extremely high transaction costs

. . .

Too much information for each individual to independently...

::: incremental
-   Gather
-   Verify
-   Prioritize
-   Contextualize
-   Structure
:::

## Some premises: institutions

Democracies benefit from non-governmental institutions that lower the transaction costs of learning what is new, true, and important.

. . .

The media is one.

. . .

Others include the scientific community/academia, political parties, interests groups, etc.

## Some premises: institutions

We use the government to lower transaction costs in some forms of economic exchange. Why not for information exchange?

. . .

Imposing conformity costs via informal norms \>\>\> imposing them via formal rules.

. . .

Empowering the government to say what is new, true, and important is empowering *whomever happens to control the government* to say what is new, true, and important.

## Some premises: market for information

Both professional and amateur (social) media tend to follow a market logic

::: incremental
-   Supply meets demand
-   Demand is not strictly oriented toward maximizing the acquisition of true information
:::

. . .

Market structure --\> information environment

## Expectations {.smaller}

Some professional norms we might want our information *producers* to abide by?

::: incremental
-   Honesty
    -   Get the facts right
-   Independence
    -   Avoid conflicts of interest
        -   With businesses
        -   With parties
        -   With government
    -   Same as neutrality? Objectivity?
-   Accountability
    -   Minimize harm
    -   Correct mistakes, allow criticism
:::

## Expectations

As these are norms, not rules, the mechanisms that sustain them are *informal*

-   Honesty
-   Independence
-   Accountability

. . .

Properties of *sources* over *time*, not individual pieces of information.

. . .

History of the media is the history of businesses adapting to *technological change* and *market pressures*

:::::: columns

Earliest newspapers in U.S. were overtly partisan

::: incremental

    -   High production costs
    -   Low demand
-   Publishers relied on partisan patrons

## Origins of the U.S. Media {.smaller}

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
Technological progress --\> "penny press"

::: incremental
-   Mass production, mass consumption
-   Less reliance on partisan patronage
    -   Can turn a profit on circulation
-   But, formal/informal favors still common
    -   Jackson / spoils system
    -   Payoffs
:::

## Yellow Journalism {.smaller}

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="70%"}
"Yellow journalism": early innovations in selling newspapers

::: incremental
-   Named for "The Yellow Kid" syndicated cartoon
-   Featured choices designed to be catchy
    -   Pictures/comics
    -   Sensational coverage (physical clickbait)
-   Pioneered by William Randolph Hearst and Joseph Pulitzer (sound familiar?)
:::
::::

::: {.column width="30%"}
![](images/yellow_kid.jpeg){fig-alt="Drawing of 'The Yellow Kid', who is bald, barefoot, holding a goblet, standing in front of an empty bottle, and wearing a yellow dress that says 'Well Hullygee Here's To You'"}

::::::

## Muckraking {.smaller}

:::::: columns

Progressive Era movement toward transparency / "good government" reforms --\> investigative journalism

::: incremental
-   Dubbed "muckraking" (derogatory) by Teddy Roosevelt
    -   Frustration with focus on negative information
-   Not always substantiated, but often spurred meaningful reforms
    -   Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906, e.g.
:::

## Professionalization

Ad-driven business model discourages "yellow" journalism. Why?

Advertisers want to protect their brands.

## Nationalization and Concentration

Current trends: fewer outlets, owned by fewer companies

Concentration --\> more common (national) content across local outlets

. . .

-   Radio: iHeartMedia
-   Local Print: Gannett
-   Local TV: Sinclair

## Nationalization and Concentration

Social media *trends toward concentration*. Why?

. . .

Network effects: people want to use the sites more other people are using

## Regulating the Media

Regulating the media in a country with strong press freedom rules/norms is tricky.

::: incremental
-   High constitutional bar for [prior restraint]{.yellow} (restricting speech before it occurs).
    -   Remember *NYT v. US* (1971) re: Pentagon Papers
-   Illegal to intentionally publish false information
    -   Proving intent is difficult
:::

. . .

Easier to regulate radio/TV (vs. print/digital) because airwaves are in limited supply

## Regulating the Media {.smaller}

Federal Communications Commission (FCC) regulates radio/TV

::: incremental
-   1949-1987: Fairness Doctrine
    -   Holders of broadcast licenses need to fairly reflect differing views on controversial issues
    -   Ruled constitutional (limited licences aren't speech), but extremely difficult to enforce
    -   Rush Limbaugh signed to syndicated contract in 1988
-   [Equal time rule]{.yellow} for *candidates* still in place, with exemptions
-   Individuals have [right of rebuttal]{.yellow} against personal attacks
:::

## Regulating the Media

Regulating the media in a country with strong press freedom rules/norms is tricky.

. . .

Digital media covered under Section 230 of Communications Decency Act

::: incremental
-   Platforms aren't publishers
-   Websites aren't legally liable for content their users post (with some exceptions)
:::

. . .

Debate over whether algorithmic recommendation counts as editorial/publisher-style intervention

Easier to achieve economy of scale to offset fixed costs, larger (and therefore more economically viable) potential audiences – easier to sell more ads at higher rates.

## Media Effects

Remember how there's no such thing as a perfect survey question?

. . .

Reporting the news is similar.

. . .

Organizations have to make *decisions* about what and how to report. Those decisions can matter a lot.

## Media Effects

:::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
Choices:

::: incremental
-   [Filtering]{.yellow}: choice of what's newsworthy
-   [Framing]{.yellow}: choice of how to present issue
:::
::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/framing_jobs.png){fig-alt="CNN, Fox Business, and New York Times headlines reporting the same jobs report. CNN: The US economy added 150,000 jobs last month. Here's what that means. ## Media Effects

Typically, news media affects what we think *about*, harder to get people to think *differently*

. . .

Remember heresthetics! Candidates try to get media to cover their preferred issues. [Examples?]{.fragment}

## Politicians and the Media

Candidates and elected officials want the media to talk about...

::: incremental
-   Them (favorably)
-   Issues favorable to them
:::

. . .

Various strategies to get [earned media]{.yellow} (as opposed to paid media) that sets the agenda

## Politicians and the Media {.smaller}

A few standard strategies:

-   [Press release]{.yellow}: official written communication
-   [Press conference]{.yellow}: open forum between official and press
-   [Press briefing]{.yellow}: more restricted forum between press secretary/communications staff and press
-   [Trial balloon]{.yellow}: anonymous disclosure of (potential) policy proposal, issue position, or other idea
-   [Leak]{.yellow}: strategic disclosure of newsworthy information on the condition that the source isn't identified

## How the Press Works: Beats

Reporters often assigned "beats" to cover on a regular basis.

. . .

Ongoing coverage of particular issue --\> expanded network of sources and accumulating expertise

![](images/dawn_vaughan_profile.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="Bio for Dawn Baumgartner Vaughan: Dawn Baumgartner Vaughan is the Capitol Bureau Chief for The News & Observer, leading coverage of the legislative and executive branches in North Carolina with a focus on the governor, General Assembly leadership and state budget. Open Government Coalition Sunshine Award and several North Carolina Press Association awards, including for politics and investigative reporting."}

## How the Press Works: Packs

Reporters are people. Reporters working the same beats talk to each other.

. . .

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
[Pack journalism]{.yellow}: when (social) network effects lead journalists from different outlets to converge on similar coverage
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/trump_af1_press.png){fig-alt="Donald Trump speaking to a gaggle of reporters on Air Force One"}
:::
:::::

## How the Press Works: The Record

Conversations are typically "on the record" unless both the source *and journalist* agree otherwise

::: incremental
-   [On the record]{.yellow}: allowing what you say to be quoted by name
-   [On background]{.yellow}: information can be used, but not attributed
-   [Off the record]{.yellow}: information cannot be used
:::

## How the Press Works: The Record

Off-record is a *mutual agreement*. Just because you say "off the record" doesn't mean it's off the record.

![](images/office_off_record.png){fig-align="center" fig-alt="The Office meme: I DECLARE OFF THE RECORD"}

## Working the Press

Journalists' interactions with political figures are repeated games.

. . .

Political figures: need to maintain credibility

Journalists: need to maintain access

-   "beat-sweetener": favorable story about a source

## You and the Media {.smaller}

You should generally be skeptical of claims that "the media" is engaged in conspiracies to manipulate views or suppress information

::: incremental
-   It's a business, supply meets demand
    -   Slant often reflects what audience wants to hear
-   It's a competitive market
    -   If it's new, true, and important there's an incentive to report on it
    -   If professional media didn't report on it, it might be difficult to verify
-   Just because you didn't see the story doesn't mean it wasn't written
-   People who claim the media has an agenda...may have an agenda
:::

## You and the Media

What is "fake" news? What does it mean for news to be "fake"?

. . .

We often mean one of...

[Misinformation]{.yellow}: Inaccurate or misleading information

[Disinformation]{.yellow}: Information produced with the *intention* to mislead

## You and the Media

Some academic debate over how big of a problem mis/disinformation is...

::: incremental
-   "Fake news" sources have tiny market share
-   Corrections work (on specific false claims)
-   Attitudes --\> misperceptions more than the other way around
:::

## You and the Media

More common phenomena:

-   Repurposing true information from reliable sources
-   Partisan curation (non-overlapping sets of true information)

## You and the Media {.smaller}

What can you do?

::: incremental
-   Look for *source-level* indicators of reliability
    -   Clear distinction between news/opinion/advertisement
    -   Transparency in ownership/funding sources
    -   Processes for verification and correction
-   Know yourself
    -   It's okay to have a perspective
    -   Easiest to be misled by what you *want* to hear
:::

## Practice multiple choice question

Which of the following illustrates institutional durability?

a.  a proposed amendment to the Constitution fails
b.  a university has the same courses and policies, but all of its students and professors have been replaced
c.  an organization establishes a budget over a ten-year time horizon
d.  two bureaucratic agencies are merged into one

. . .

[b. a university has the same courses and policies, but all of its students and professors have been replaced]{.yellow}

## Practice multiple choice question

Which of the following correctly describes a function of the House Rules Committee?

a.  it ensures that proposed bills don't conflict with other laws that Congress doesn't intend to change
b.  it turns general policy goals submitted by members into precise legal language
c.  it establishes rules for members' behavior in matters such as etiquette, decorum, and ethics
d.  it determines when and how a bill may be amended

. . .

[d. it determines when and how a bill may be amended]{.yellow}

## Practice short answer question {.smaller}

One of labor unions' main activities is negotiating "collective bargaining agreements," which set standards for things like wages and benefits for all workers rather than each employee negotiating these items independently. In some states, it is illegal to require workers to pay union dues as a condition of their employment – even if their wages and benefits will be set by a collective bargaining agreement. This policy is often referred to as "right to work."

It stands to reason that unions oppose right to work laws, but – in the language of collective action – why?

. . .

[Right to work laws create free rider problems, allowing workers to get the benefits of collective bargaining agreements without paying costs associated with negotiating them.]{.yellow}
